_: One line per object for the hover card. Widely published facts, worded to stay true as measurements are refined. Keyed by the name used in assets/skylabels.json.
Sirius: The brightest star in the night sky: a white star twice the Sun's mass, with a white-dwarf companion that was once the bigger of the two.
Canopus: Second-brightest star in the sky, a yellow-white supergiant; spacecraft have used it as a fixed point for navigation.
Arcturus: Brightest star of the northern sky, an orange giant moving fast across our view — it is a visitor from an older part of the Galaxy.
Vega: Once the pole star, around 12,000 BCE, and will be again; the first star ever photographed, in 1850.
Capella: Looks like one star, is two yellow giants circling each other in about 104 days, too close for any telescope to separate.
Rigel: A blue supergiant tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun; the brightest star in Orion despite its name meaning the foot.
Procyon: Rises just before Sirius, hence the name 'before the dog'; one of the Sun's nearest bright neighbours.
Betelgeuse: A red supergiant so large it would swallow the orbit of Mars if it sat where the Sun is; expected to explode as a supernova within the next hundred thousand years.
Achernar: Spins so fast it is flattened into an oval, its equator bulging far wider than its poles — one of the least spherical stars known.
Hadar: A hot blue triple star; with Alpha Centauri it forms the 'pointers' to the Southern Cross.
Altair: Rotates once in under ten hours, fast enough to flatten it noticeably; one of the closest bright stars, seen as it was about 17 years ago.
Acrux: The bottom star of the Southern Cross, a multiple system of hot blue stars; it appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil and others.
Aldebaran: The red eye of Taurus, an orange giant that only appears to sit among the Hyades cluster — it is less than half as far away.
Antares: The heart of the Scorpion, a red supergiant whose name means 'rival of Mars' for its colour.
Spica: Two hot blue stars so close they orbit in four days and distort each other's shape; by watching it Hipparchus discovered the precession of the equinoxes.
Pollux: The brighter of the Gemini twins, an orange giant with a planet found in 2006.
Fomalhaut: Ringed by a vast disc of dust; the first star around which a planet was photographed directly, in 2008.
Deneb: One of the most luminous stars visible to the eye — it looks first-magnitude from more than a thousand light-years away.
Mimosa: Second-brightest star of the Southern Cross, a hot blue giant that pulses slightly every few hours.
Regulus: The heart of the Lion, lying almost on the Sun's path across the sky, so the Moon and planets pass close to it.
Adhara: Would be the brightest star in the sky by far to anyone seeing in ultraviolet.
Castor: Six stars in one: three pairs, all bound together, seen as a single point.
Gacrux: The top of the Southern Cross, a red giant close enough for its colour to show against the blue of its neighbours.
Shaula: The Scorpion's sting; its name means 'raised tail'.
Bellatrix: The 'Amazon star', Orion's left shoulder, a hot blue giant.
Elnath: The tip of the Bull's horn, once shared with the constellation Auriga.
Alnilam: The middle star of Orion's Belt, a blue supergiant far more distant than the other two.
Alnair: The brightest star of the Crane, a hot blue star used in celestial navigation.
Alnitak: The easternmost star of Orion's Belt, beside the Horsehead and Flame nebulae.
Alioth: Brightest star of the Big Dipper; its magnetic field sorts elements into patches on its surface.
Dubhe: One of the two 'pointer' stars of the Big Dipper that lead the eye to Polaris.
Mirfak: Brightest star in Perseus, a yellow-white supergiant at the heart of a loose cluster of young stars.
Wezen: A yellow supergiant so luminous it shines second magnitude from about 1,600 light-years.
Kaus Australis: The brightest star in Sagittarius, the southern part of the Archer's bow.
Avior: One of the stars of the 'false cross', often mistaken for the Southern Cross.
Alkaid: The end of the Big Dipper's handle; unlike most of the Dipper it is not part of the moving group the others share.
Menkalinan: Two nearly identical stars eclipsing each other every four days.
Atria: The brightest star of the Southern Triangle, an orange giant.
Alhena: The foot of Pollux in Gemini, a subgiant beginning to swell as its core runs out of hydrogen.
Peacock: Named in 1930 by the Royal Air Force, which wanted every navigation star to have a proper name.
Mirzam: Rises just ahead of Sirius; the name means 'the herald'.
Polaris: The North Star: it sits almost exactly over the Earth's axis, so it barely moves while every other star wheels around it. It is a Cepheid, pulsing every four days.
Alphard: The 'solitary one', the only bright star in a large empty stretch of sky.
Hamal: The head of the Ram; four thousand years ago the Sun stood here at the spring equinox, which is why the zodiac still starts at Aries.
Algieba: A close pair of golden giants, one of the finest double stars for a small telescope.
Diphda: The tail of the Whale; the brightest star in Cetus, an orange giant.
Nunki: A hot blue star in the Teapot of Sagittarius, near the direction of the Galaxy's centre.
Menkent: An orange giant in Centaurus, and one of the nearer bright stars to the Sun.
Alpheratz: Shared for centuries between Pegasus and Andromeda; now the head of Andromeda.
Saiph: Orion's right knee, a blue supergiant hotter than Rigel but fainter to the eye because most of its light is ultraviolet.
Mizar: The middle of the Dipper's handle, with faint Alcor beside it — an ancient eyesight test — and itself the first double star found with a telescope.
Algol: The 'Demon Star': every 2.87 days a dimmer companion passes in front and it fades for ten hours, a change visible to the eye and known since antiquity.
Rasalhague: The head of the Serpent Bearer, spinning so fast its shape is flattened.
Kochab: The brighter of the two 'guardians of the pole'; it was the pole star around 1500 BCE.
Almach: A gold and blue double star, one of the most colourful in a small telescope.
Denebola: The Lion's tail; a young star with a disc of dust around it.
Alphecca: The jewel of the Northern Crown, an eclipsing pair.
Mira: The 'wonderful' star: swells and fades over eleven months from easy naked-eye brightness to invisibility, and trails a tail of gas thirteen light-years long.
Caph: One of the five stars of Cassiopeia's W; a fast-spinning yellow-white giant.
Shedar: The brightest star of Cassiopeia, an orange giant at the chair's lower corner.
Mirach: A red giant used as a stepping stone to find the Andromeda Galaxy.
Menkar: The jaw of the Whale, a red giant near the end of its life.
Alcyone: The brightest of the Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, a cluster of young blue stars born together.
Albireo: One star to the eye, gold and blue in any telescope: the most famous coloured double.
Sadr: The heart of the Swan, at the centre of the Northern Cross.
Enif: The nose of Pegasus, an orange supergiant.
Scheat: A red giant in the Great Square of Pegasus whose brightness wanders irregularly.
Markab: One corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.
Ankaa: The brightest star of the Phoenix, an orange giant.
Alderamin: Will be the pole star around the year 7500.
Etamin: The brightest star in Draco; the star James Bradley watched when he discovered the aberration of light in 1728, the first direct proof that the Earth moves.
Rastaban: The Dragon's eye, a yellow giant.
Thuban: The pole star when the pyramids were built, around 2700 BCE.
Sabik: A close pair of hot stars in Ophiuchus.
Zubeneschamali: The northern claw of the Scorpion, now in Libra; sometimes reported as looking faintly green, which no other star does.
Zubenelgenubi: The southern claw of the Scorpion, now in Libra, a wide double for binoculars.
Unukalhai: The heart of the Serpent, an orange giant.
Cor Caroli: Named for King Charles of England; a strongly magnetic star with a chemically peculiar surface.
Arneb: The brightest star of the Hare beneath Orion, a yellow-white supergiant.
Phact: The brightest star of the Dove.
Naos: One of the hottest stars visible to the naked eye, far bluer and more luminous than the Sun.
Aludra: The tail of the Great Dog, a blue supergiant.
Suhail: A bright orange supergiant in Vela, the Sails.
Miaplacidus: Second-brightest star in Carina, a blue-white giant; its name means 'placid waters'.
Aspidiske: One of the stars of the 'false cross' in Carina.
Alsephina: Part of the 'false cross', a pair of hot blue stars in Vela.
Markeb: One of the four stars of the 'false cross'.
Sargas: In the Scorpion's tail, a yellow-white giant.
Girtab: One of the stars of the Scorpion's sting.
Ascella: In the Teapot of Sagittarius, a close pair of stars.
Kaus Media: The middle of the Archer's bow.
Kaus Borealis: The northern end of the Archer's bow.
Alnasl: The tip of the Archer's arrow, pointing at the centre of the Galaxy.
Tarazed: A neighbour of Altair in the Eagle, an orange giant.
Sualocin: 'Nicolaus' backwards: named after the assistant who inserted his own name into a star catalogue in 1814.
Rotanev: 'Venator' backwards: the second half of the smuggled name Nicolaus Venator, in Delphinus.
Sadalmelik: The 'lucky star of the king', a yellow supergiant in Aquarius.
Sadalsuud: The 'luckiest of the lucky', a yellow supergiant in Aquarius.
Skat: The shin of the Water Bearer.
Deneb Algedi: The tail of the Sea Goat, an eclipsing pair.
Moon: Our Moon, drawn at its true distance, size and phase for this moment.
Sun: Our star, drawn at its true apparent size: half a degree across, the same width as the full Moon.
Mercury: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun; a day there lasts longer than its year.
Venus: The brightest planet, hidden under clouds of sulphuric acid; hotter at the surface than Mercury.
Mars: The red planet; its colour is rust. Home to the tallest volcano in the Solar System.
Jupiter: The largest planet, with more than twice the mass of all the others combined; its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the Earth.
Saturn: The ringed planet; its rings are mostly water ice and would fit between the Earth and the Moon.
Andromeda Galaxy: The nearest large galaxy, a trillion stars; the most distant thing visible to the naked eye. It will merge with our Galaxy in about four billion years.
Triangulum Galaxy: The third-largest galaxy of our Local Group, visible to the eye from a truly dark site.
Orion Nebula: A cloud of gas where stars are being born now; visible to the eye as the fuzzy middle star of Orion's sword.
Pleiades: The Seven Sisters: a cluster of hot young stars born together about a hundred million years ago, still wrapped in a faint blue haze.
Hyades: The nearest star cluster to the Sun, the V-shaped face of the Bull.
Praesepe: The Beehive: a swarm of stars in Cancer that Galileo was the first to resolve.
Large Magellanic Cloud: A companion galaxy to our own, visible from the southern hemisphere as a detached patch of the Milky Way.
Small Magellanic Cloud: A dwarf galaxy orbiting ours, where Henrietta Leavitt found the star law that made it possible to measure the size of the universe.
47 Tuc: One of the brightest globular clusters: a million stars in a ball, older than the Solar System.
ω Cen Cluster: Omega Centauri: the largest globular cluster in the Galaxy, possibly the core of a swallowed dwarf galaxy.
Lagoon Nebula: A star-forming cloud in Sagittarius, one of the few nebulae visible to the naked eye.
Eagle Nebula: Home of the 'Pillars of Creation', the columns of gas photographed by the Hubble telescope.
η Car Nebula: The Carina Nebula, one of the largest star-forming regions in the sky, home to a star that once flared to become the second-brightest in the heavens.
Coathanger: An accidental line of stars that looks exactly like a coat hanger in binoculars; not a true cluster.
Southern Pleiades: A bright, loose cluster in Carina, a southern counterpart to the Pleiades.
h Persei: One half of the Double Cluster in Perseus, two young clusters side by side, visible to the eye.
χ Persei: One half of the Double Cluster in Perseus, two young clusters side by side, visible to the eye.
Butterfly Cluster: An open cluster in Scorpius whose brighter stars trace a butterfly's wings.
Ptolemy's Cluster: Recorded by Ptolemy in the year 130 as a 'nebula following the sting of Scorpius'.
Rosette Nebula: A ring of glowing gas around a cluster of hot young stars that carved the hole in its middle.
GalCtr: The centre of the Milky Way: a black hole of four million solar masses, hidden behind dust in Sagittarius.
Coma Star Cluster: A loose scattering of stars once counted as the tuft of the Lion's tail.
α Persei Cluster: A loose cluster of young stars around Mirfak, spanning several degrees of sky.
Diamond Cluster: A small, bright cluster in Vela.
Wishing Well Cluster: A rich open cluster in Carina, like coins at the bottom of a well.
Crab Globular Cluster: A globular cluster in Cancer, a ball of ancient stars.
Stinging Scorpion Cluster: A bright open cluster in Scorpius.
False Comet Nebula: A patch of clusters and nebulosity in the Scorpion's tail that has fooled observers into reporting a comet.
Fox Fur Nebula: A nebula in Monoceros beside the Christmas Tree Cluster.
τ CMa Cluster: An open cluster in Canis Major around the star Tau Canis Majoris.
ο Vel Cluster: A cluster in Vela around Omicron Velorum.
Cr 140: A loose open cluster in Canis Major.
